items.sentence_raw: Students who want to enter the University of Montreal's Athletic Complex need more than just a conventional ID card - their identities must be authenticated by an electronic hand scanner.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says *'Students who want to enter the University of Montreal's Athletic Complex'* need an *'electronic hand scanner'*. So **sports students** use a **hand scanner**.

items.sentence_raw: In some California housing estates, a key alone is insufficient to get someone in the door; his or her voice print must also be verified.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says in *'some California housing estates'*, a *'voice print must also be verified'* to enter. So **home owners** use a **voiceprint** system.

items.sentence_raw: And soon, customers at some Japanese banks will have to present their faces for scanning before they can enter the building and withdraw their money.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says *'customers at some Japanese banks will have to present their faces for scanning'*. So **bank customers** will use a **face scanner**.

items.sentence_raw: All of these are applications of biometrics, a little-known but fast-growing technology that involves the use of physical or biological characteristics to identify individuals.
In use for more than a decade at some high-security government institutions in the United States and Canada, biometrics are now rapidly popping up in the everyday world.
Already, more than 10,000 facilities, from prisons to day-care centres, monitor people's fingerprints or other physical parts to ensure that they are who they claim to be.
Some 60 biometric companies around the world pulled in at least $22 million last year and that grand total is expected to mushroom to at least $50 million by 1999.
items.explain: Q27: Paragraph B gives numbers: *'$22 million last year'* and *'expected to mushroom to at least $50 million'*. These **figures** show the money side of the story. So the heading **'The figures say it all'** fits perfectly.

items.sentence_raw: Biometric security systems operate by storing a digitised record of some unique human feature.
items.explain: Q28: Paragraph C explains the process: the system *'stores a digitised record'* and then *'scans the person's corresponding characteristics'* to match them. This is exactly answering the question **'How does it work?'**.

items.sentence_raw: When an authorised user wishes to enter or use the facility, the system scans the person's corresponding characteristics and attempts to match them against those on record.
items.explain: Q28: Paragraph C explains the process: the system *'stores a digitised record'* and then *'scans the person's corresponding characteristics'* to match them. This is exactly answering the question **'How does it work?'**.

items.sentence_raw: Systems using fingerprints, hands, voices, irises, retinas and faces are already on the market.
Others using typing patterns and even body odours are in various stages of development.
Fingerprint scanners are currently the most widely deployed type of biometric application, thanks to their growing use over the last 20 years by law-enforcement agencies.
Sixteen American states now use biometric fingerprint verification systems to check that people claiming welfare payments are genuine.
items.explain:
Q29: Paragraph D says systems check *'that people claiming welfare payments are genuine'*. This is about stopping people from getting money they shouldn't — which is **'Fighting fraud'**.

Q37: The passage says *'Sixteen American states now use biometric fingerprint verification systems to check that people claiming welfare payments are genuine'*. So **welfare claimants** use a **fingerprint scanner**.

items.sentence_raw: In June, politicians in Toronto voted to do the same, with a pilot project beginning next year.
To date, the most widely used commercial biometric system is the handkey, a type of hand scanner which reads the unique shape, size and irregularities of people's hands.
items.explain: Q30: Paragraph E states the handkey is *'the most widely used commercial biometric system'*. **'Most widely used'** means it **'sells best'** in the market. So the heading is **'This type sells best in the shops'**.

items.sentence_raw: Originally developed for nuclear powerplants, the handkey received its big break when it was used to control access to the Olympic Village in Atlanta by more than 65,000 athletes, trainers and support staff.
items.explain: Q35: The passage explains the handkey *'was used to control access to the Olympic Village in Atlanta by more than 65,000 athletes'*. So **Olympic athletes** used a **hand scanner**.

items.sentence_raw: Now there are scores of other applications.
Around the world, the market is growing rapidly.
Malaysia, for example, is preparing to equip all of its airports with biometric face scanners to match passengers with luggage.
items.explain:
Q31: Paragraph F gives specific future plans: *'Malaysia... is preparing to equip all of its airports'* and *'Japan's largest maker... is developing new machines'*. These are examples of **'Who's planning what'**.

Q36: The passage states *'Malaysia... is preparing to equip all of its airports with biometric face scanners to match passengers with luggage'*. So **airline passengers** will use a **face scanner**.

items.sentence_raw: And Japan's largest maker of cash dispensers is developing new machines that incorporate iris scanners.
items.explain: Q31: Paragraph F gives specific future plans: *'Malaysia... is preparing to equip all of its airports'* and *'Japan's largest maker... is developing new machines'*. These are examples of **'Who's planning what'**.

items.sentence_raw: The first commercial biometric, a hand reader used by an American firm to monitor employee attendance, was introduced in 1974.
items.explain: Q38: The passage mentions *'a hand reader used by an American firm to monitor employee attendance'*. So **business employees** use a **hand scanner** for work.

items.sentence_raw: But only in the past few years has the technology improved enough for the prices to drop sufficiently to make them commercially viable.
"When we started four years ago, I had to explain to everyone what a biometric is," says one marketing expert.
"Now, there's much more awareness out there."
Not surprisingly, biometrics raise thorny questions about privacy and the potential for abuse.
items.explain: Q32: Paragraph G starts by saying biometrics *'raise thorny questions about privacy and the potential for abuse'*. **'Thorny questions'** and **'privacy'** worries are **'Common objections'** people have.

items.sentence_raw: Some worry that governments and industry will be tempted to use the technology to monitor individual behaviour.

"If someone used your fingerprints to match your health-insurance records with a credit-card record showing you regularly bought lots of cigarettes and fatty foods," says one policy analyst, "you would see your insurance payments go through the roof."
In Toronto, critics of the welfare fingerprint plan complained that it would stigmatise recipients by forcing them to submit to a procedure widely identified with criminals.
Nonetheless, support for biometrics is growing in Toronto as it is in many other communities.
In an increasingly crowded and complicated world, biometrics may well be a technology whose time has come.
items.explain: Q33: Paragraph H concludes that *'biometrics may well be a technology whose time has come'*. This means people are starting to accept it as unavoidable — they are **'Accepting the inevitable'**.
